q952: From the beginning God said, "It is not good that the man should be alone" (Genesis 2:18). Scripture shows people needing each other in hard times. When Moses grew weary in battle, Aaron and Hur held up his hands until the victory came (Exodus 17:12). Ecclesiastes 4:10 warns, "woe to him that is alone when he falleth." Paul tells us, "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2). Even Jesus, in the garden of Gethsemane, asked His friends to stay and watch with Him (Matthew 26:38). Reaching out follows this pattern. When you are struggling, asking a safe person for help is not weakness but obedience to God's design, allowing His love to come to you through His people.
q953: Humans are wired for connection. When we are with a trusted person, research suggests our brains respond to threat less strongly. In one study, people anticipating a mild shock showed less activity in stress-related brain areas while holding the hand of a loved one. This is called co-regulation, where one calm nervous system helps settle another. Connection can also involve hormones like oxytocin, which supports bonding and reduces stress responses. Loneliness, on the other hand, is linked in studies with higher stress hormones and poorer health. Sending a short, specific message such as asking for ten minutes makes reaching out easier and less overwhelming. Over weeks, practising this builds a network of support and teaches your brain that help is available and safe to ask for.
q954: God is relational at His very core, Father, Son and Holy Spirit in perfect love. He made us in His image, designed to live in relationship. That is why connection heals and isolation harms. When we reach out to others, we open ourselves to receive God's comfort through human faces and voices. This reflects His humility and generosity. He chooses to work through ordinary people, inviting us to share in His work of caring for each other. It also reflects His wisdom in creating a body where each part needs the others. Asking for help gives others the chance to love, and receiving it heals our sense of being alone. Over time, these honest connections become part of the way God restores us to wholeness and joy.
q955: The Bible connects peace with our bodies, not only our thoughts. "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety" (Psalm 4:8). Psalm 127:2 reminds us that God gives His beloved sleep, so anxious toil is not needed. Jesus invited the weary to take His yoke, saying, "I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls" (Matthew 11:29). Paul teaches that our bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19), worthy of care. Progressive muscle relaxation follows this pattern. As you tense and release each muscle group, you let go of tension you have been carrying and allow your body to rest in God's safe keeping.
q956: When we are stressed, our muscles tighten without our noticing, especially in the jaw, shoulders and neck. This tension sends signals back to the brain that something is wrong, keeping the stress response going. Progressive muscle relaxation interrupts this loop. By tensing a muscle group for a few seconds and then releasing it, you create a clear contrast that helps the brain notice what relaxation feels like. The release lowers signals from the muscles to the brain, which helps calm the nervous system. Studies suggest this practice can reduce anxiety, improve sleep and ease tension headaches. Finishing with slow breaths adds the calming effect of the vagus nerve. Practised regularly over weeks, the body learns to relax more quickly and stays less tense during the day.
q957: God created our bodies to respond to stress and then recover, but in modern life many of us stay tense for long periods. Progressive muscle relaxation is one way He has provided for us to return to rest. By designing our muscles to relax more deeply after being tensed, God made a simple way for us to experience release. This reflects His understanding of our frame and His desire for our wellbeing. It also teaches a spiritual truth. Sometimes we only realise how much we are holding when we feel the contrast of letting go. As you practise, you can offer each area of tension to God, trusting His care. Over time, this habit helps your body and soul rest more fully in His peace.
q958: The Bible celebrates the human body as God's careful work. David praised God, saying, "I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works" (Psalm 139:14). He also recognised that God formed his inward parts in the womb (Psalm 139:13). Paul prayed that our whole spirit, soul and body would be kept blameless (1 Thessalonians 5:23), showing that the body matters to God. In Romans 12:1 we are urged to present our bodies as a living sacrifice. A body scan follows this pattern. By slowly paying attention to each part of your body without judgement, you honour it as God's creation and become more aware of what it is telling you. You can also invite God to search and know you, body and soul.
q959: Your brain constantly receives signals from the body about heartbeat, breathing, tension, hunger and more. The ability to notice these signals is called interoception, and an area called the insula helps process them. Many people, especially those who have faced stress or trauma, become disconnected from their bodies. A body scan gently trains attention to notice sensations again. Research suggests regular practice may strengthen interoceptive awareness, helping people recognise emotions earlier and respond with less reactivity. Noticing without judging matters, because criticism can trigger stress. When you find tension and breathe into it, you add a calming effect through the vagus nerve. Over weeks of practice, people often feel more at home in their bodies and better able to understand their feelings and needs.
q960: God did not make us as spirits trapped in bodies but as whole persons, spirit, soul and body together. Our bodies are not enemies or mere machines but part of who we are. By designing us so that kind attention to the body brings calm and understanding, God shows that He values every part of us. This reflects His love and care for our physical lives. Jesus took on a human body, healed bodies and rose with a body, honouring them for ever. Practising a body scan is a way of receiving your body as a gift and listening to it with gratitude. Over time, this helps you live more fully, notice your needs and care for yourself wisely, so you can love God and others with your whole being.
q961: The Bible teaches that what we believe shapes how we live. Paul urges, "be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind" (Romans 12:2). Jesus said, "ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free" (John 8:32). In Lamentations, after describing deep despair, the writer chooses to remember God's faithfulness: "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope" (Lamentations 3:21). Philippians 4:8 directs us to think on what is true and honest. A thought record follows this pattern. By writing down a painful thought and checking the evidence, you test it against reality and God's truth. This is not denying feelings but bringing them into the light so that truth can reshape them.
q962: When something upsetting happens, automatic thoughts often appear so quickly we barely notice them. These thoughts can be distorted, such as assuming the worst, thinking in all-or-nothing terms or reading other people's minds. They strongly influence our emotions and actions. Writing them down slows the process and engages the prefrontal cortex, which can evaluate and reframe them. Looking for evidence for and against helps break the habit of accepting every thought as true. Creating a balanced thought and re-rating the feeling shows how changing the thought changes the emotion. Research suggests this approach is one of the most effective for anxiety and depression. Over weeks of practice, the brain begins to form new pathways, so balanced thinking becomes more automatic in everyday life.
q963: God created us with the ability to reason, reflect and choose what to believe. This gift allows us to grow, learn and be transformed. In a broken world our thoughts can become twisted by pain, fear or lies, but God has given us ways to correct them. A thought record is one practical tool that works with this design. It reflects His love for truth and His desire for us to live in freedom. It also reflects His patience, since changing thought patterns takes time and practice. As you learn to test your thoughts and align them with reality and Scripture, your emotions and relationships often become healthier. Over time, this renewal of mind helps you live more fully in the hope and peace God offers.
q964: Jesus spoke directly to worry. "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof" (Matthew 6:34). He reminded His listeners that the Father feeds the birds and clothes the lilies (Matthew 6:25-33). David wrote, "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice" (Psalm 55:17), and Daniel prayed three times a day at set times (Daniel 6:10). Worry time follows this pattern. Instead of letting worry fill every moment, you set aside a specific time to bring your concerns to God. During the rest of the day you gently say later, trusting that He holds tomorrow.
q965: Worry often feels uncontrollable because it can appear at any time and spread into every part of the day. Setting a fixed worry time helps the brain learn that worries can wait. When you write a worry down and postpone it, you reduce the habit of mental rehearsal and give your mind permission to focus on the present. Studies suggest that this kind of postponement reduces the amount and intensity of worry. During worry time, sorting concerns into solvable and unsolvable helps the brain move from endless thinking to action or acceptance. Keeping it away from bedtime protects sleep. Ending on time teaches the mind that worry has limits. Practised over weeks, many people find their worries become less frequent and less overwhelming.
q966: God made us as creatures living in time, with days and nights, work and rest. He never meant for us to carry the weight of the future all at once. Worry time reflects this design by placing concerns within limits, so they do not take over our lives. It also reflects His invitation to bring our burdens to Him in prayer. By setting aside a time to face worries honestly, we are not ignoring them but handing them to God in an orderly way. This shows His wisdom and care for our minds. He knows that endless worry harms us, and He offers a better way. Over time, this practice can help you live more peacefully in the present, trusting God for each day.
q967: The Bible encourages us to keep doing good even when we feel weary. "Let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not" (Galatians 6:9). Psalm 37:3 tells us to trust in the LORD and do good. When the man by the pool of Bethesda had been ill for many years, Jesus told him, "Rise, take up thy bed, and walk" (John 5:8), inviting him into action as part of his healing. In Psalm 42:4 David remembered the joy of going with others to worship, recalling past activities that gave him life. Behavioural activation follows this pattern. It invites you to take small steps of action, trusting that God can restore joy and strength through them.
q968: Depression often reduces energy and motivation, which leads to doing less. Doing less then reduces opportunities for pleasure and achievement, which can deepen low mood. This creates a downward cycle. Behavioural activation breaks this pattern by scheduling small activities that give enjoyment or a sense of accomplishment. When you do them, even without feeling motivated, the brain's reward system can begin to respond again. Over time, this can help restore pathways linked with motivation and pleasure. Research suggests behavioural activation is an effective treatment for depression, comparable to other well-known therapies. Rating your mood before and after helps you see the connection between action and feeling. Practised over weeks, small activities can gradually lift mood and increase energy. If depression is severe, it is wise to seek professional help.
q969: God created us to live, work, rest and enjoy His world. When we stop engaging in life, our hearts and bodies often suffer. Behavioural activation reflects God's design that action and feeling are connected. He made our brains to respond to meaningful activity, so even small steps can bring change. This reflects His grace. He does not require us to feel strong before acting. He meets us in our weakness and gives strength as we take small steps of faith. It also reflects His love for joy and purpose. Activities that bring pleasure or a sense of achievement remind us that life is a gift. Over time, these small steps can help restore hope, energy and a renewed sense of God's goodness in everyday life.
q970: Scripture often shows faithful people deciding before the moment of testing arrives. Daniel 1:8 says that Daniel "purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself", and he made that choice before the king's food was ever set in front of him. Proverbs 21:5 praises the thoughtful plans of the diligent, and Psalm 119:11 describes hiding God's word in the heart ahead of time so that it is ready when temptation comes. Proverbs 16:9 adds a gentle balance: we plan our way, but the LORD directs our steps. An if-then plan is simply this biblical pattern made practical. You name the cue, you choose the faithful response, and you invite God into the moment before it comes. He meets us not only in the struggle itself but in the quiet preparation that comes first.
